terms.def: A station that listens on one frequency and at the same time retransmits what it hears on another, extending the range of other stations.
terms.more: To call a known station on one, say that station's call sign, then your own. To invite a contact, give your call sign followed by the word "listening".

terms.def: The difference between a repeater's transmit frequency and its receive frequency.
terms.more: Common offsets: plus or minus 600 kHz on the 2-meter band and plus or minus 5 MHz on the 70-centimeter band. An improper offset can keep you from accessing a repeater you can hear.

terms.def: The frequency on which a repeater listens, which is the frequency you transmit on to use it.
terms.more: The reverse function on a transceiver lets you listen on the repeater's input frequency.

terms.def: The frequency on which a repeater transmits, which is the frequency you listen on to hear it.
terms.more: Hearing the output does not mean you can get in: a wrong offset, CTCSS tone or DCS code will each keep the repeater from responding to you.

terms.def: A transceiver feature that swaps your repeater transmit and receive frequencies.
terms.more: Its purpose is to listen on a repeater's input frequency, which lets you tell whether you can hear the other station directly.

terms.def: A radio that combines a transmitter and a receiver in one unit.
terms.more: A VHF/UHF transceiver must be set to the right offset to reach a repeater. Its reverse function lets you listen on the repeater's input frequency.

terms.def: A network of repeaters in which signals received by one repeater are transmitted by all the repeaters in the network.
terms.more: Linking makes the repeaters act as one system that covers a much larger area.

terms.def: The amateur VHF band from 144 to 148 MHz.
terms.more: A common repeater offset here is plus or minus 600 kHz. The national calling frequency for FM simplex is 146.520 MHz.

terms.def: The amateur UHF band from 420 to 450 MHz.
terms.more: A common repeater offset here is plus or minus 5 MHz.

terms.def: Very high frequency: the part of the radio spectrum from 30 to 300 MHz.
terms.more: The 2-meter band is VHF. VHF/UHF band plans designate simplex channels so stations in range of each other need not tie up a repeater.

terms.def: Ultra high frequency: the part of the radio spectrum from 300 to 3000 MHz.
terms.more: The 70-centimeter band is UHF. VHF/UHF band plans designate simplex channels so stations in range of each other need not tie up a repeater.

terms.def: The number of times a radio wave vibrates each second, which is the place on the dial where a signal is found.
terms.more: It is measured in hertz. No station owns a frequency: two stations interfering on the same one should negotiate continued use of it.

terms.def: Kilohertz: a unit of frequency equal to one thousand hertz.
terms.more: A common repeater offset in the 2-meter band is plus or minus 600 kHz.

terms.def: Megahertz: a unit of frequency equal to one million hertz, or one thousand kilohertz.
terms.more: 146.520 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency on 2 meters. A common 70-centimeter repeater offset is plus or minus 5 MHz.

terms.def: Transmitting and receiving on the same frequency, with stations talking directly to each other and taking turns.
terms.more: No repeater is involved. Band plans designate simplex channels so stations within range of each other can communicate without tying up a repeater.

terms.def: An agreed frequency where stations listen for each other and make first contact.
terms.more: For FM simplex operations in the 2-meter band it is 146.520 MHz.

terms.def: Frequency modulation: a mode in which your voice changes the frequency of the transmitted signal.
terms.more: It is the usual voice mode on VHF/UHF repeaters and simplex. Talking too loudly makes FM audio drop out on voice peaks.

terms.def: How far an FM signal's frequency swings as you speak.
terms.more: A louder voice gives more deviation. Talking too loudly causes too much of it, and your audio drops out on voice peaks.

terms.def: Voice transmission: any mode in which you speak into a microphone.
terms.more: To seek a call from any phone station when not using a repeater, repeat "CQ" a few times, say "this is" and your call sign, then pause to listen.

terms.def: The unique set of letters and a digit that identifies a licensed station.
terms.more: When calling or answering, say the other station's call sign first, then your own.

terms.def: A general call that means "calling any station".
terms.more: To answer one, transmit the other station's call sign followed by your own. On a repeater it is customary to say your call sign and "listening" instead.

terms.def: A short standard signal with an agreed meaning that helps manage a contact.
terms.more: "CQ" is a procedural signal meaning calling any station.

terms.def: A voluntary guideline for using different modes or activities within an amateur band.
terms.more: It goes beyond the privileges established by the FCC. VHF/UHF band plans designate simplex channels, for example.

terms.def: A receiver function that mutes the audio when a signal is not present.
terms.more: Ordinary squelch opens for any signal. With CTCSS, the squelch opens only for signals that carry the right sub-audible tone.

terms.def: Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System: a sub-audible tone transmitted along with normal voice audio to open the squelch of a receiver.
terms.more: Many repeaters require one. Using the wrong CTCSS tone is one reason you may be unable to access a repeater whose output you can hear.

terms.def: Digital Coded Squelch: a digital code sent with your signal that a receiver or repeater must see before it opens.
terms.more: Using the wrong DCS code is one reason you may be unable to access a repeater whose output you can hear.

terms.def: Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency: signaling that sends two audio tones at the same time for each key pressed on a keypad.
terms.more: It is the type of signaling to a repeater that uses two simultaneous audio tones. CTCSS, in contrast, is one continuous sub-audible tone.

terms.def: Digital Mobile Radio: a digital voice system used on some amateur repeaters.
terms.more: It uses talkgroups to organize radio traffic and a color code that your transmitter must send to access a specific repeater.

terms.def: An identifier used by DMR to organize radio traffic so that those who want to hear the group are not bothered by other radio traffic.
terms.more: To join one, program your radio with the group's ID or code.

terms.def: An access code that must be programmed into a DMR transmitter to access a specific repeater.
terms.more: It plays a role like the CTCSS tone on an FM repeater: without the matching code the repeater does not respond.

terms.def: Unwanted signals that get in the way of the signal you are trying to receive.
terms.more: When two stations on the same frequency interfere with each other, they should negotiate continued use of the frequency. Interference from other stations is reported as QRM.

terms.def: A three-letter code beginning with Q that stands for a common phrase or question.
terms.more: QRM means you are receiving interference from other stations. QSY means you are changing frequency.

terms.def: The Q signal meaning that you are receiving interference from other stations.
terms.more: Memory aid: M for man-made. Compare QRN, which is static noise from natural sources.

terms.def: The Q signal meaning that you are changing frequency.
terms.more: Hams use it when moving a contact to another frequency.

terms.def: The part of the FCC rules that governs the Amateur Radio Service in the United States.
terms.more: FCC rules always apply to the operation of an amateur station, including during emergency work. RACES is itself a Part 97 service.

terms.def: Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service: an FCC Part 97 amateur radio service for civil defense communications during national emergencies.
terms.more: It requires certification by a civil defense agency. ARES is a separate, voluntary program that does not.

terms.def: Amateur Radio Emergency Service: a group of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for communications duty in the public service.
terms.more: Unlike RACES, it does not require certification by a civil defense agency. FCC rules still apply to its operations.

terms.def: An organized on-the-air meeting of stations, run by a net control station.
terms.more: Standard practice: unless you are reporting an emergency, transmit only when directed by the net control station.

terms.def: The station that runs a net: it calls the net to order and directs communications between the stations checking in.
terms.more: Other stations transmit only when it directs them to, unless they are reporting an emergency.

terms.def: Announcing your station to the net control station so that you are counted as taking part in a net.
terms.more: The net control station directs communications between the stations checking in.

terms.def: Formal messages exchanged by net stations.
terms.more: A formal traffic message begins with a preamble, which contains the information needed to track the message.

terms.def: A formal written message passed by amateur radio in a standard format.
terms.more: Its header includes the preamble, used to track the message, and the check, which is the number of words in the text.

terms.def: The opening part of a formal traffic message, which contains the information needed to track the message.
terms.more: The recipient's address and telephone number are not part of it.

terms.def: In a radiogram header, the number of words or word equivalents in the text portion of the message.
terms.more: The receiving operator counts the words copied and compares the count with it to confirm that nothing was lost.

terms.def: A set of standard words that stand for letters (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie) so that spelled letters are understood clearly by voice.
terms.more: Spelling words with a standard phonetic alphabet is the technique used to make sure voice messages containing unusual words are received correctly.

terms.def: A system that relays messages by amateur radio using email addresses based on amateur call signs.
terms.more: It is a message delivery system, not just a digital mode like FT8 or PSK31.

terms.def: Communications needed when human life is in immediate danger or property needs immediate protection.
terms.more: In such situations a control operator may operate outside the frequency privileges of their license class. In a net, reporting an emergency is the one reason to transmit without being directed.

terms.def: The frequencies on which a licensed operator is allowed to transmit, set by license class.
terms.more: You may operate outside them only in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property.

terms.def: The licensed amateur who is responsible for a station's transmissions.
terms.more: Control operators must stay within the frequency privileges of their license class, except in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property.
